planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil. Minuteman arose as a sport of the popular Francee hosta, with crisper white variegation and a more vigorous, upright habit.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously and watering well until established. Minuteman is a sport of the widely grown Francee hosta, distinguished by a crisper, brighter white margin around a dark green, heart-shaped leaf and a more vigorous, upright, vase-shaped clump that holds its variegation well without fading in summer heat. Lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in mid to late summer, but the bold two-tone foliage carries most of the ornamental value from spring through frost. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on the tender new growth, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in early spring.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container plants in early spring in any well-drained soil; multiflora rose is classified as a noxious weed in many U.S. states because it naturalizes aggressively from bird-dispersed hips — confirm it is legal to plant in your area before choosing it.

directions: This East Asian species rose was widely planted through the mid-20th century in the U.S. as a living fence, wildlife cover, and rootstock for grafted garden roses, forming a huge, thorny, sprawling mound covered in clusters of small, single, white to pale pink, fragrant flowers in late spring followed by abundant small red hips. It is now considered a serious invasive species across much of the eastern and midwestern U.S., since birds spread the hips widely and seedlings establish readily in pastures, fencerows, and woodland edges, so verify local regulations before planting and consider a non-invasive alternative such as a named rambler or shrub rose bred from it. Where legal and wanted for wildlife plantings, it needs no supplemental water once established and tolerates poor soil, but requires a large, unmanicured space since it cannot be kept small by pruning. Cut plants resprout vigorously from the base, so removal of unwanted volunteers requires repeated cutting or herbicide treatment of the stump.
sources: USDA Forest Service — Fire Effects Information System

common_name: Bishop's Dahlia (Species Dahlia, Parent of the Bishop Series)

planting.note: Plant tubers or transplants after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Dahlia merckii is the wild species behind the popular dark-leaved Bishop series such as Bishop of Llandaff.

directions: Plant tubers 4-6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, or set out started plants once nights stay reliably above 50°F. Dahlia merckii is a slender, airy, wild Mexican species dahlia that grows taller and looser than modern bedding hybrids, producing masses of small, single, lilac-pink to white flowers with a bright yellow center on wiry stems from midsummer into fall, and it is the parent species behind the dark-foliaged Bishop series of garden dahlias. Stake the tall, wind-prone stems in exposed sites, and pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth and more flowering stems. In zones below 8, lift and store tubers indoors over winter in a frost-free location, replanting in spring; where hardy, mulch heavily to protect the crown from hard freezes.

common_name: Lindley's Butterfly Bush (Weeping Purple Buddleja Species)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Lindley's butterfly bush is a spreading, suckering species that dies back to the ground in colder parts of its range and regrows from the roots each spring.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it room to spread since this species suckers and colonizes an area over time rather than staying in a tidy clump. Lindley's butterfly bush produces distinctive one-sided, arching racemes of small tubular reddish-purple flowers from summer into fall, a looser and more graceful bloom form than the dense conical spikes of the common Buddleja davidii, and it attracts butterflies and hummingbirds just as readily. In the northern part of its hardiness range it behaves as a woody-based perennial, dying back to the ground each winter and resprouting vigorously in spring, so cut old stems to the ground in late winter to keep growth tidy. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established and needs little care beyond an annual hard pruning and removal of unwanted suckers at the edge of the planting.
